title: Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner
articleTitle: The Judicial Refinement of the Research and Development Tax Credit: A Comprehensive Analysis of Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner and the Evolving Standards for Engineering Firms
subject: Process of Experimentation
summary: In Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113, the U.S. Tax Court denied a Tennessee MEPF engineering firm's federal R&D tax credits under IRC § 41, finding none of three sample projects involved qualified research. For engineering and architecture firms, the key takeaway: routine design calculations and generic time records cannot substantiate the credit.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary and Case Background
Overview of the Litigation and Holding

On December 23, 2024, the United States Tax Court issued a landmark Memorandum Opinion in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (Docket No. 4759-22), authored by Judge Travis A. Greaves. The decision represents one of the most stringent judicial examinations of the federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credit under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 41 as applied to architectural, engineering, and construction (AEC) and mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and fire protection (MEPF) consulting firms.

The Tax Court ruled entirely in favor of the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, holding that Phoenix Design Group, Inc. (PDG) failed to establish that any of the three representative projects selected for trial involved "qualified research" within the meaning of IRC § 41(d). Furthermore, enforcing a pretrial stipulation executed by the parties, the Court sustained the Internal Revenue Service's (IRS) imposition of 20% accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662 across all deficiency years. The ruling establishes a rigorous evidentiary benchmark in the United States, requiring engineering firms to distinguish routine professional design services, standard thermodynamic and load calculations, and municipal building code compliance from genuine hypothesis-driven scientific experimentation.
Taxpayer Profile and Operational Workflow

Phoenix Design Group, Inc. is a Tennessee-based professional engineering consulting firm incorporated and taxed as a C corporation. Founded in 1997 by professional engineers Ross T. Malloy, Thomas Fisher, and Clyde Searcy, the firm was structured so that experienced principal engineers could remain directly engaged in hands-on technical design work rather than purely administrative management. During the tax years at issue (2013 through 2016), PDG's principals—Ross T. Malloy, Thomas Fisher, John Wade, Jerry Young, and Brian Moore—oversaw the design of complex MEPF systems incorporated into acute-care hospitals, medical laboratories, academic research buildings, and educational facilities.

Across its project portfolio, PDG asserted that its engineering operations followed a standardized, six-stage design process that purportedly mirrored the scientific method. The workflow commenced with the Basis of Design Stage, in which engineers gathered high-level functional, spatial, and operational requirements from the building owner and lead architect, and progressed into the Schematic Design Stage, where the architect began determining the building footprint and created gross block diagrams, while PDG engineers analyzed this initial information to estimate the appropriate MEPF systems, established contact with utilities to determine how to connect the building to existing infrastructure, and provided the architect with preliminary locations for the MEPF systems. During the subsequent Design Development Stage, the project architect provided plans incorporating PDG's preliminary MEPF locations, which PDG engineers used to determine the best route for the HVAC system, adjust the MEPF systems to accommodate changes in building size, work with local zoning authorities, and develop alternative systems and run feasibility calculations, with the architect or owner determining which system to incorporate. In the Construction Document Stage, the building owner determined final equipment selection (such as imaging systems), PDG engineers relied on manufacturers' cut sheets to ensure the MEPF systems could support that equipment and ran final load calculations, and PDG produced stamped construction documents for use by contractors and review by code officials. Finally, during the Bidding Stage, the building owner or architect solicited bids from construction contractors and the owner could request that PDG revise the design to minimize costs, leading into the Construction Administration Stage, where physical construction commenced and PDG reviewed contractor shop drawings, responded to requests for information (RFIs), and verified field installations.
The Taxpayer's R&D Credit Claim and the IRS Challenge

PDG provided documentation on all projects it undertook between 2012 and 2016, from which its third-party consultant, alliantgroup (engaged on February 1, 2017), identified 419 possible projects that qualified for research credits. After removing all projects known not to contain qualifying activities and de minimis projects, alliantgroup reduced the population of potentially qualifying projects for the IRC § 41 Credit for Increasing Research Activities to 238. The consultant then analyzed a sample of these projects and issued a report to PDG (the opinion does not state the size of that sample or the extrapolation methodology used), and the resulting qualified research expenses (QREs) were attributable solely to wages paid to PDG's employees.

Based on the alliantgroup reports, PDG claimed $562,798 in federal R&D tax credits generated during tax years ended December 31, 2013, through December 31, 2016 (claimed on amended 2014 through 2016 returns, with the 2013 credit carried forward on the amended 2014 Form 3800 because PDG did not amend its 2013 return), and utilized $535,455 of those credits on its federal corporate income tax returns for tax years 2015 through 2019. Following an examination of PDG's 2015 through 2019 returns, the IRS issued a notice of deficiency on December 14, 2021, disallowing the research credits, determining deficiencies totaling $461,741, and determining $91,806 in accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662.

body.text: To manage the litigation burden of over 200 disputed projects, the parties agreed to try a nonbinding sample of three trial projects. The trial was structured to establish an analytical framework enabling the parties to resolve their differences across the remaining project population without trying all 238 projects individually. Crucially, the parties entered into a binding all-or-nothing stipulation regarding the IRC § 6662 penalties: if the Tax Court held that at least one of the three sample projects entailed qualified research under IRC § 41, the Commissioner would concede all accuracy-related penalties across all tax years. Conversely, if the Court held that none of the three sample projects involved qualified research, PDG stipulated that it would be liable for an accuracy-related penalty for each credit year in which there is a deficiency determined by the Court or by agreement of the parties.

body.text: Governing United States Statutory and Regulatory Framework

In the United States, a taxpayer claiming the research tax credit under IRC § 41(a) bears the burden of proving under Tax Court Rule 142(a) that its claimed QREs (such as in-house employee wages under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), supplies under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), or 65% of contract research expenses under IRC § 41(b)(3)) were paid or incurred in carrying on a trade or business for "qualified research". Under IRC § 41(d)(1), activities constitute "qualified research" only if the taxpayer satisfies each element of a cumulative Four-Part Test applied separately to each distinct "business component".

First, under the Section 174 Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)), the expenditures must be eligible for treatment as research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174. Pursuant to Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), expenditures qualify only if they represent R&D costs in the "experimental or laboratory sense"—meaning activities intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product. Objective uncertainty exists only if the information available to the taxpayer at the outset does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the product, or the appropriate design of the product. While IRC § 174 permitted an elective current deduction under IRC § 174(a) during the 2013–2016 research years at issue in Phoenix Design Group, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, Pub. L. 115-97, subsequently mandated five-year domestic amortization for post-2021 Specified Research or Experimental (SRE) expenditures, a rule later modified for post-2024 domestic expenditures through the enactment of IRC § 174A under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025, Pub. L. 119-21 (signed July 4, 2025), which restored an immediate deduction for domestic research or experimental expenditures in tax years beginning after December 31, 2024; throughout these statutory evolutions, however, the substantive threshold of uncertainty under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2 remains the foundational prerequisite for IRC § 41 eligibility.

Second, under the Technological in Nature Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i)), the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature (in Phoenix Design Group, the Commissioner conceded this test as well as the business component test, so the Court examined only the Section 174 test and the process of experimentation test). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4), information is technological in nature only if the process of experimentation used to discover such information fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science, rather than social sciences, arts, humanities, or commercial management.

Third, under the Business Component and Permitted Purpose Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii)), the taxpayer must intend to apply the discovered technological information to develop a new or improved "business component," which IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) defines as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. Under IRC § 41(d)(3)(A)—which the Court in Phoenix Design Group treated as the final element of the process of experimentation test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), rather than as part of the business component test—the research must be undertaken for a qualified purpose—specifically, to create a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality—whereas research relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors is statutorily excluded under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B).

Fourth, under the Process of Experimentation Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C)), "substantially all" of the research activities with respect to the business component must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), the "substantially all" mandate is satisfied only if 80% or more of a taxpayer's research activities, measured on a cost or another consistently applied reasonable basis (such as employee hours), constitute elements of a process of experimentation. Pursuant to Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5), a process of experimentation is a structured evaluative process designed to assess one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability, method, or appropriate design is uncertain at the outset. The taxpayer must undertake a systematic progression of work akin to the scientific method—identifying the specific technical uncertainty, formulating hypotheses or design alternatives, and conducting modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error to test and analyze those alternatives.

If an overarching business component (such as an entire building's MEPF system) fails the Four-Part Test, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2)—the shrinking-back rule—mandates that the requirements be applied to the "most significant subset of elements" of the product or system, continuing downward to progressively smaller subcomponents until either a qualifying subcomponent is isolated or the most basic element of the product fails to qualify. Finally, taxpayers are required under IRC § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) to maintain sufficient contemporaneous books and records to substantiate both the qualitative eligibility of the claimed subcomponents and the quantitative nexus connecting employee hours and wages to those specific subcomponents.
2. Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

Judge Greaves' opinion in Phoenix Design Group systematically dismantled the taxpayer's evidentiary presentation, resting its holding on the Section 174 test and the process of experimentation test (the Commissioner having conceded the technological information and business component tests); the five dimensions discussed below include a fifth, contractual dimension that the Court did not decide. Analyzing the exact mechanics of these failures provides essential guidance for tax attorneys and technical advisors structuring and defending engineering research credit claims.
Failure to Establish Objective Technological Uncertainty Under IRC Section 174

The primary fatal flaw in PDG's litigation posture was its conflation of project-level factual unknowns and iterative design evolution with objective technological uncertainty under IRC § 174 and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1). PDG argued that because every hospital and university laboratory building has a unique architectural footprint and custom utility requirements, the appropriate design of the entire MEPF system was uncertain at the outset of each engagement and remained uncertain because design drawings were revised throughout construction.

The Tax Court rejected this theory by drawing a sharp legal distinction between system-wide uncertainty and subcomponent uncertainty under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(5). Relying on recent precedent in Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84, and Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15, aff'd, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), Judge Greaves held that objective uncertainty regarding a discrete subcomponent does not necessarily render the basic design specifications of the entire system uncertain. For example, uncertainty regarding the diffuser placement in the hybrid operating room or the final equipment selection in BHNM Oxford, or the strict airflow requirements of the imaging suite in VU ESB, did not create uncertainty across the entire hospital or university MEPF system. PDG relied on sparse, conclusory witness testimony and failed to demonstrate technically how localized subcomponent adjustments altered or destabilized the fundamental engineering architecture of the whole MEPF system.

Furthermore, the Court found that PDG failed to demonstrate what specific technical information was unavailable to its engineers at project inception. Under the Section 174 test, a taxpayer must prove that the information objectively available to it at the outset did not establish the capability, method, or appropriate design. In the Gerald Champion project, the medical center provided PDG at the outset with existing schematic design documents from prior engineering firms, a gross block diagram showing general building locations, and historical utility data for sizing equipment. PDG failed to prove that these initial schematic diagrams and historical data were insufficient to establish the basic design of the MEPF systems.

Similarly, in the BHNM Oxford and VU ESB projects, PDG claimed uncertainty existed because the buildings were new construction—in BHNM Oxford, the engineers did not initially know the footprint of the hospital or the final equipment to be selected, and in VU ESB, the specific use of each portion of the building had not been determined. Judge Greaves ruled that the schematic block diagram and preliminary master plan provided by the architect resolved the claimed footprint uncertainty in BHNM Oxford; that, although there may have been objective uncertainty as to equipment selection, PDG engineers simply waited for Baptist Memorial's final selection and reran load calculations, which is not a process of experimentation; and that in VU ESB, Vanderbilt University—not PDG—resolved the uncertainty regarding the use of each portion of the building, so PDG did not engage in investigative activities to resolve it. The opinion's findings of fact also recount that in BHNM Oxford the hospital requested that PDG electrical engineers use a "Powerwave Bus System" to power its information technology data center. PDG electrical engineers met with the vendor to learn how the commercial bus system worked, consulted with the hospital to determine what servers and equipment would be housed in the IT room, and, together with the mechanical engineers responsible for cooling the room, determined the configuration of the equipment, after which the manufacturer built systems to meet the expected demand. The Court did not separately analyze the Powerwave Bus System; it held more generally that, as to the decisions encountered by PDG electrical engineers, PDG failed to show any investigative activities, and it noted that while meeting with third parties to solicit information can be an investigative activity (citing Betz), merely meeting with them and relaying their options to the client does not amount to a process of experimentation under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C).
Absence of a Structured Process of Experimentation Under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C)

Even if PDG had established uncertainty under IRC § 174, the Tax Court held that PDG failed to prove that its engineers engaged in a "process of experimentation" under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5). PDG's central defense rested on the assertion that its standard six-stage engineering workflow (Basis of Design, Schematic Design, Design Development, Construction Documents, Bidding, and Construction Administration) formed an iterative loop mirroring the scientific method. Citing Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, Judge Greaves rejected this formalistic argument, holding that a taxpayer cannot satisfy the process of experimentation test merely by attaching activities to a generalized multi-stage business plan that superficially resembles the scientific method. Instead, the Court must evaluate the actual activities performed by specific engineers. Worse still, the evidentiary record revealed that PDG's employees did not categorize their hours by those six design stages, nor did the time log descriptions align with the work supposedly completed in each stage, leading Judge Greaves to express skepticism that PDG employees even followed the described six-stage process in practice.

In evaluating the actual engineering activities performed, the Court drew a decisive doctrinal boundary between performing standard engineering calculations on available data and conducting investigative experimentation. In the Gerald Champion project, PDG mechanical engineers reviewed existing HVAC drawings and discovered a major flaw: prior engineers had failed to account for the hospital's high elevation, which reduces air density and alters the volumetric airflow required to reach target heating and cooling temperatures. After calculating the heating and cooling loads, PDG determined that the existing HVAC system could support the renovation area but not the small addition, prompting them to design a new air handling system for the addition. In doing so, the engineers considered a constant air volume (CAV) system versus a variable air volume (VAV) system (selecting VAV for individual room temperature control), evaluated using chilled water from the hospital's central plant versus a standalone refrigeration system (selecting a local system after pipe sizing calculations showed existing plumbing was insufficient), and determined that connecting to a hospital-wide refrigerant loop on the opposite side of the building for heat rejection was not cost-efficient.

Judge Greaves ruled that none of these engineering decisions constituted a process of experimentation. Performing calculations and communicating the results to the architect is not an evaluative process that mirrors the scientific method, and, as the Court explained (citing Betz, which involved calculations to determine duct size based on airflow), performing basic calculations on available data is not an investigative activity because the taxpayer already has all the information necessary to address the unknown. Furthermore, choosing between well-understood HVAC configurations (such as CAV versus VAV or central chilled water versus local refrigeration) based on standard load calculations and cost-efficiency reflects the exercise of general professional engineering expertise rather than a scientific course of study or hypothesis testing.

The Court also highlighted how non-scientific and excluded factors drove PDG's workflow. In Gerald Champion, after PDG mechanical engineers calculated the approximate size of the HVAC equipment using historical data, they reported those dimensions to the project architect, who decided to place the system in a mechanical room based on aesthetics. Not only does reporting sizing calculations to an architect fail to reflect the scientific method, but design choices governed by aesthetics are statutorily excluded from qualified purposes under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B). Similarly, with respect to building codes, the Court noted in BHNM Oxford that PDG did not develop its code-based uncertainty argument to any significant extent and that all systems designed by PDG engineers are subject to a building code, and in VU ESB it found that PDG offered only conclusory statements that all the systems affected LEED Silver certification, without evidence of the systems' interdependence. Finally, in VU ESB, PDG asserted that its electrical engineers conducted a formal "study" with Vanderbilt University; however, Judge Greaves noted that while a study might theoretically mirror the scientific method, PDG failed to provide sufficient evidence detailing the activities involved in the study or the extent of PDG electrical engineers' involvement, precluding a finding of experimentation.
Failure of the Substantially All Mandate and Collapse of the Shrinking-Back Rule

Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), at least 80% of a taxpayer's research activities measured on a cost or time basis with respect to a business component must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose. Because PDG defined its business component holistically as the MEPF systems as a whole for each building, the whole-system claims failed the Section 174 test, and the Court added that, even if PDG had satisfied the Section 174 test, PDG failed to provide sufficient information to determine whether it satisfied the 80% "substantially all" threshold at the whole-building level.

When the holistic MEPF systems failed the Four-Part Test, Judge Greaves examined whether subsets of the projects could be salvaged under the shrinking-back rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2). In doing so, the Tax Court articulated a vital legal limitation on how a business component may be shrunk back. PDG argued that if an entire building's MEPF system failed, the Court could shrink the business component back into specific chronological design phases (such as the Schematic Design or Design Development stage) or into the activities of specific employees. Judge Greaves accepted shrinking back by discipline as consistent with the regulatory text but rejected the design-phase and employee approaches because they ignore the requirement of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) to apply the test to the next most significant subset of elements of the business component—in these projects, PDG engineers worked on various subsets of the MEPF systems in each design stage (for example, roof units and the fire alarm system in the same BHNM Oxford design stage, and lighting work spanning several stages), and no employee focused exclusively on one subset (for example, Thomas Fisher worked on both the chiller and steam distribution issues in VU ESB, and Ross T. Malloy also worked on the steam distribution issue); accordingly, a failed MEPF system could shrink back into the mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems and, if the record allowed, into further subsets of those systems, but on these facts never into a design phase or an individual employee.

Following this proper hierarchy, Judge Greaves first evaluated the Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing systems individually across each of the three trial projects and concluded that none of the individual disciplines satisfied the Four-Part Test as a whole. When Judge Greaves then attempted to apply the shrinking-back rule one level deeper—to the "next most significant subset" (specific subcomponents) of each mechanical, electrical, and plumbing system—PDG's claim collapsed completely due to inadequate time and activity documentation. Because PDG's hour logs recorded employee time using broad discipline labels or vague task descriptions rather than subcomponent-specific codes, the Court could not identify which specific subsets the engineers worked on or how many hours were spent on any discrete subcomponent. Consequently, the Court could not verify whether the activities on any subcomponent were investigative, part of a process of experimentation, or performed for a permitted purpose, rendering the shrinking-back rule futile.
Fatal Recordkeeping Defects, Statistical Sampling Flaws, and Impeachment of Witness Testimony

The Phoenix Design Group ruling underscores that the taxpayer bears the burden of proof under Tax Court Rule 142(a): the Court found PDG's testimony sparse and conclusory, rejected testimony that was directly refuted by the hour sheets, and held that the records PDG did provide were too generic to substantiate qualified research. Across all three trial projects, PDG's internal employee "hour sheets" suffered from pervasive vagueness. In Gerald Champion, employees recorded time to high-level categories such as "HVAC," "lighting/power system design," and "work on plumbing fixtures" without linking hours to discrete technical uncertainties. In BHNM Oxford, PDG employees logged a total of 16,650 hours—including 5,941 hours in the mechanical discipline, 5,876 hours in the electrical discipline, 4,333 hours in the plumbing discipline, 501 hours in generic project phases without a specified discipline, with CAD designers accounting for 2,118 of the total hours (261 mechanical, 947 electrical, 909 plumbing, and 1 construction administration)—yet provided no subcomponent breakdown. Similarly, in VU ESB, key engineers logged significant time under opaque descriptions: mechanical engineer John Beard recorded significant time simply to "design," electrical engineer Brian Moore recorded time to "project coordination," and plumbing engineer Raymond Parham recorded time to "ABP". PDG failed to provide any quantitative allocation metric to bridge these generic time entries to the specific engineering challenges discussed by witnesses at trial.

Judge Greaves expressed particular skepticism toward the veracity and reliability of the hour sheets submitted for Project No. 12010.01 (VU ESB / Olin Hall) due to six specific evidentiary defects uncovered in the trial record. First, PDG engineers recorded substantial time in 2013 and 2014, long before PDG executed its September 29, 2015 fixed-fee contract ($1,758,500) with Wilson Architects for the modified VU ESB project. Second, Vanderbilt University had originally contracted with Wilson Architects (who subcontracted PDG on July 17, 2013) to design an interdisciplinary "TEAM building" containing biomedical labs and a vivarium, but work was halted when the medical center withdrew from the joint venture; Vanderbilt subsequently executed a new contract with Wilson Architects on January 1, 2014, removing the biomedical portions and vivarium while retaining a five-story laboratory structure, a 10,000-square-foot ground-floor cleanroom, and two basement levels housing nanoscale/atomic-level microscope imaging suites. Because PDG failed to establish the exact date the prior TEAM building project was halted, the Court could not verify whether the 2013–2014 hours belonged to the abandoned TEAM building or the VU ESB project. Third, PDG's assertion that no subprojects were recorded under Project No. 12010.01 was directly contradicted by subproject entries appearing on the hour sheets. Fourth, the hour sheets contained time entries from 2017, which lay outside the 2013–2016 tax credit years at issue. Fifth, the generic time descriptions ("design," "project coordination," "ABP") lacked any allocation metric. Sixth, and most damaging to witness credibility, Ross T. Malloy testified at trial that only Ross T. Malloy, Thomas Fisher, and Ryan Malloy worked on the Vanderbilt campus steam distribution system tie-in; however, the contemporaneous hour sheets revealed that CAD designer Barry Septer also recorded time explicitly referencing the steam line—directly refuting the witnesses' testimony.

Compounding the defects in the hour sheets, PDG submitted periodic revisions of design drawings and equipment selection schedules (such as the September 26, 2013 design drawings and project manual in Gerald Champion and plumbing drawings in BHNM Oxford) into the evidentiary record without documentary or testimonial explanation of why or how the revisions were made. Judge Greaves noted that, as aptly summarized by PDG's own counsel, the unexplained design drawings "tell[] me nothing" regarding the actual activities performed by the engineers to arrive at the solutions. Because PDG failed to establish that any qualified research occurred and because the parties had narrowed the trial to whether the projects entailed qualified research rather than the amount of QREs, the Tax Court (which did not address the estimation rule of Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930)) held that none of the three trial projects, as a whole or at the shrinking-back level, involved qualified research and held PDG liable for the accuracy-related penalties, while expressly not determining the amounts of the deficiencies, consistent with the parties' stipulation.
Contractual Architecture and Funded Research Vulnerabilities in MEPF Engagements

Although the Tax Court resolved Phoenix Design Group entirely on the taxpayer's failure to satisfy the Four-Part Test and substantiation requirements under IRC § 41(d)—making a separate holding on the "funded research" exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) unnecessary—the contractual arrangements documented in Judge Greaves' opinion highlight critical legal vulnerabilities that govern AEC and MEPF contracts. In Gerald Champion, PDG agreed to design and update the MEPF systems for a fixed compensation of $90,000, payable upon the completion of specified design and construction milestones. In VU ESB, PDG executed a sub-agreement with Wilson Architects on September 29, 2015, for a fixed fee of $1,758,500 to design the MEPF and telecommunication systems starting at the Design Development phase.

When evaluated alongside parallel United States judicial authorities such as Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024), Populous Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner, Docket No. 405-17 (T.C. Dec. 6, 2019) (order), System Technologies, Inc. v. Commissioner, Docket No. 12211-21, and Smith v. Commissioner, Docket Nos. 13382-17 et al., these contractual structures present two major hazards. First, entering a contract at the Design Development phase (because earlier design work had already been performed on the predecessor project, as in VU ESB) or contracting to deliver code-compliant blueprints across standard American Institute of Architects (AIA) milestones frames the engineer's legal duty as rendering "proper performance" of routine professional services rather than achieving an uncertain technical research result. Second, under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), research performed under contract is excluded as "funded research" unless the taxpayer both bears the financial risk of technical failure (such that compensation is contingent on the technical success of the research rather than unconditional milestone progress billing for services) and retains substantial rights in the research results (meaning the taxpayer retains the right to use the underlying technical discoveries in future engagements without paying royalties or surrendering exclusive intellectual property ownership to the client). Standard fixed-fee milestone contracts that lack explicit technical acceptance testing, refund remedies for unsuccessful research, or clear demarcation between client ownership of physical blueprints and engineer retention of underlying technical discoveries remain acutely vulnerable to disqualification under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H).
3. Comparative Summary Table: Statutory Requirements vs. Taxpayer Failures and Judicial Standards

The following table maps each statutory and regulatory requirement examined in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner against PDG's specific evidentiary failures and the controlling standard of proof enforced by the U.S. Tax Court.

headers: Taxpayer's Specific Failure in Phoenix Design Group
Tax Court's Standard of Proof and Controlling Principle

cells: 1. Definition of Business Component

PDG defined its business components holistically as the entire building-wide MEPF system for each hospital or university facility (the mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems together); the Commissioner conceded the business component test, and the whole-system component instead failed the Section 174 test.

A business component must be a distinct product, process, software, technique, formula, or invention. Claiming an entire facility's MEPF system requires proving that the entire system (not merely an isolated room or subsystem) satisfies every prong of the Four-Part Test.
2. Elimination of Objective Technical Uncertainty (Section 174 Test)
IRC § 41(d)(1)(A); IRC § 174(a); Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) & (a)(5)

PDG claimed system-wide uncertainty because architectural footprints were initially unknown, the hybrid operating room and final equipment selection created uncertainty, and drawings were revised during construction. In Gerald Champion, PDG failed to show that the initial gross-block diagram, schematic design diagrams, and historical data provided at the outset did not establish the basic design.

The taxpayer must identify specific technical information unavailable at project outset showing that existing knowledge, historical data, and schematic diagrams could not establish capability, method, or appropriate design. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(5), uncertainty in a subcomponent does not render the whole system uncertain.
3. Technological in Nature

Not a ground of decision: the Commissioner conceded the technological information test, and the Court refused to extend that concession to the separate investigative-activities requirement of the Section 174 test. Activities discussed elsewhere in this report—such as meeting with the Powerwave Bus System vendor, project coordination ("ABP"), and deferring to an architect's aesthetic room placement.

The discovery process must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4)); because this prong was conceded, Phoenix Design Group did not apply it to PDG's activities.
4. Permitted Purpose (Function, Performance, Reliability, Quality)

In Gerald Champion, mechanical room placement was dictated by the architect based on aesthetics. Because the hour sheets could not be tied to specific subcomponents, the Court was unable to determine whether PDG's activities were for a permitted purpose; it also found PDG's building-code (BHNM Oxford) and LEED Silver (VU ESB) uncertainty arguments undeveloped or conclusory.

Activities must specifically target a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of the business component. Research related to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal factors is not for a qualified purpose (IRC § 41(d)(3)(B)); the Court did not reach the IRC § 41(d)(4) exclusions, including the adaptation exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(B).
5. Process of Experimentation

PDG relied on its six-stage design process—which it described as iterative rather than linear—as per se proof of experimentation. Engineers performed standard thermodynamic load and elevation airflow calculations using historical data and chose between standard CAV/VAV and local/central cooling systems using professional experience. In VU ESB, PDG asserted an unverified "study".

Formalistic multi-stage design frameworks do not establish experimentation (Union Carbide). Performing standard engineering calculations on available data is not investigative because the mathematical method is already known. Taxpayers must prove a scientific-method progression: formulating hypotheses, modeling/simulating or testing uncertain alternatives, and analyzing test data.
6. "Substantially All" (80%) Quantitative Threshold

PDG failed to provide sufficient information (it supplied only the hours worked by each employee on each project) to allow the Court to determine whether 80% or more of the activities on each business component constituted elements of a process of experimentation.

At least 80% of all research activities (measured on a cost or time basis) applied to the defined business component must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose (Little Sandy Coal).
7. Shrinking-Back Rule Application

PDG argued the Court could shrink back to design phases or specific employees. When the Court properly attempted to shrink back to Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing disciplines and their subcomponents, PDG's generic time logs prevented isolating hours by subcomponent.

Shrinking back must proceed to the next most significant subset of elements (disciplines, then further subsets of each system); the Court would apply it never to chronological design phases or employee roles on this record, because PDG's work on each subset spanned multiple design stages and multiple employees. To survive at the subcomponent level, time and technical records must be segregated by subcomponent.
8. Contemporaneous Books and Records & Witness Credibility
IRC § 6001; Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d)

PDG submitted unexplained blueprint revisions ("tell[s] me nothing") and generic hour sheets ("design," "project coordination," "ABP"). VU ESB logs contained pre-contract 2013–2014 hours, possible TEAM building hours that could not be ruled out, time admittedly belonging to the steam line relocation project (No. 12010.04), 2017 out-of-scope hours, and CAD logs (Barry Septer) that directly contradicted witness testimony on the steam line tie-in.

The taxpayer bears the burden of proof; conclusory testimony is insufficient, and testimony directly refuted by the hour sheets was not credited. Unexplained drawings carry zero evidentiary weight. Where records lack an allocation metric, shrinking back is futile; the opinion does not discuss the Cohan rule, as the trial was limited to whether qualified research occurred rather than QRE amounts.
9. Accuracy-Related Penalties & Sampling Stipulations

PDG's claim rested on a consultant study of a sample drawn from 238 potentially qualifying projects, and PDG stipulated that penalties would apply if none of the three trial projects involved qualified research.

The Court imposed the accuracy-related penalties solely by operation of the parties' stipulation, without separately analyzing negligence, substantial understatement, or reasonable cause, and without determining the deficiency amounts.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how United States taxpayers and tax advisors can operationalize the holdings of Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, the following two industry case studies reconstruct realistic engineering engagements that confront the exact factual, contractual, and evidentiary pitfalls identified by Judge Greaves. Each case study details step-by-step how the taxpayer can restructure its project governance, technical documentation, commercial contract terms, and experimentation tracking to satisfy the statutory mandates of IRC §§ 41, 174, and 6001.
Case Study 1: Specialized Healthcare and Cleanroom MEPF Engineering Firm
Scenario and Alignment with Phoenix Design Group Pitfalls

Aegis Bio-Mechanical Engineering, Inc. ("Aegis"), a domestic C corporation employing 85 licensed professional engineers (PEs) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) specialists, is engaged as a sub-consultant by a prime architectural firm to engineer the MEPF infrastructure for the University Translational Nanomedicine & Surgical Center ("UTNSC"). The facility is a seven-story, 250,000-square-foot building housing standard faculty offices, general instructional classrooms, an acute-care Hybrid Intraoperative MRI Operating Suite, a 12,000-square-foot ISO Class 4 Cleanroom and Nanoscale Electron Microscopy Vault in the sub-basement, and a High-Plume Toxic Chemical Laboratory Exhaust Manifold coupled with a Campus High-Pressure Steam-to-Cryogenic Heat Recovery Tie-In.

If Aegis follows PDG's flawed approach—claiming the entire UTNSC building MEPF package as a single monolithic business component, executing a standard AIA C401 fixed-fee milestone sub-agreement at the Design Development stage, logging employee hours to generic task codes ("UTNSC – Mechanical Design," "Project Coordination," "Cleanroom Consult"), and submitting revised AutoCAD/Revit sheets without narrative analysis—the IRS and Tax Court will disallow 100% of the claim under Phoenix Design Group. Specifically, the inclusion of routine office and classroom MEPF work will cause the building-wide business component to fail both the Section 174 uncertainty test (under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(5)) and the 80% "substantially all" threshold (under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C)), while generic time tracking will prevent the Court from applying the Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) shrinking-back rule to isolate the three genuinely experimental subsystems.
Step 1: Project Governance and Pre-Design Business Component Architecture

Rather than treating the entire UTNSC building or Aegis's six-stage AIA design workflow as the business component, Aegis restructures its project governance at initial project intake (prior to Schematic Design) by establishing a Subcomponent Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) mapped directly to Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(5). Under this governance protocol, Aegis formally segregates approximately 75% of the building's MEPF scope—comprising standard office VAV boxes, restroom plumbing, code-minimum fire sprinklers, commercial IT room vendor bus systems, general lighting panels, and LEED certification checklists—into Non-Qualifying WBS Codes (Series 100), on which zero R&D tax credits are claimed.

Simultaneously, Aegis charters three standalone, physical subcomponent business components under Experimental WBS Codes (Series 900), ensuring that each subcomponent is defined as a discrete functional subsystem and evaluated independently under the Four-Part Test. The first chartered subcomponent, designated BC-901, is the Sub-Basement ISO Class 4 Laminar Air-Curtain and Ultra-Low Acoustic/Electromagnetic Isolation HVAC Subsystem, which must maintain vibrational velocity below and thermal stability within for atomic-scale electron microscopes while achieving 600 air changes per hour (ACH) without inducing turbulent eddy currents. The second subcomponent, designated BC-902, is the Hybrid Intraoperative MRI Non-Ferromagnetic Cryogenic Quench Vent and Multi-Zone Pressure-Cascade Plume Scrubber, which must safely evacuate rapid helium gas expansion during a superconducting magnet quench within a constrained interstitial ceiling plenum while maintaining positive surgical sterility pressure gradients. The third subcomponent, designated BC-903, is the Variable-Momentum Regenerative Lab Exhaust Plume Dispersion and Superheated Steam Tie-In Manifold, which must prevent toxic fume re-entrainment into adjacent hospital helipad intake louvers under turbulent urban wind-shear conditions while recovering waste heat from a fluctuating 150-psig campus steam main.
Step 2: Technical Documentation and Contemporaneous Recordkeeping

To overcome Judge Greaves' ruling that standard calculations on available data do not establish objective uncertainty or experimentation, Aegis mandates the contemporaneous creation of three engineering artifacts for each Series 900 subcomponent. First, prior to commencing design on BC-901, BC-902, or BC-903, the lead PE authors a formal Pre-Design Unavailable Information and Baseline Failure Memorandum to satisfy IRC § 174 and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1). This memorandum documents the exact baseline information provided by the client and architect (schematic block diagrams, ASHRAE handbook formulas, historical load tables, and vendor cut-sheets) and proves mathematically why those existing methods cannot establish an appropriate design. For BC-901, the memorandum demonstrates that standard ASHRAE laminar ceiling diffusers operating at 600 ACH generate acoustic pressure waves exceeding and structural micro-vibrations that breach the electron microscope's tolerance, proving objective design uncertainty at project outset.

Second, to satisfy the Process of Experimentation mandate under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5), Aegis replaces linear load sizing with a Hypothesis-Driven CFD Simulation and Alternative Evaluation Log. For BC-901, engineers formulate competing technical hypotheses—such as testing a perforated dual-plenum fabric displacement diffuser with active piezoelectric acoustic damping against an asymmetric micro-nozzle honeycomb array—and construct 3D finite-element ANSYS Fluent CFD models to simulate thermal plumes, Brownian particle dispersion, and fluid-structure acoustic resonance across four geometric alternatives (Iterations A, B, C, and D). When Iterations A and B fail in simulation due to corner vortex shedding causing localized thermal drift of , and Iteration C fails static pressure-drop constraints before Iteration D succeeds, every simulation mesh, boundary condition, quantitative output table, and rejection rationale is contemporaneously archived. Third, to cure the "tell[s] me nothing" blueprint defect identified by Judge Greaves, Aegis configures its Revit/AutoCAD environment so that every drawing revision cloud on a Series 900 subcomponent embeds mandatory metadata linking the geometric change directly to the specific CFD simulation run ID and technical hypothesis that necessitated the revision.
Step 3: Restructuring Contract Terms to Overcome Funded Research and Proper Performance Objections

To prevent the IRS from disqualifying the subcomponents as routine "proper performance" or as "funded research" under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), Aegis replaces its standard AIA C401 fixed-fee milestone contract with a bifurcated Performance-Contingent Engineering and Technical Development Sub-Agreement. First, to avoid the pre-contract and commingled-project time defects that undermined the VU ESB project, Aegis executes the written contract prior to logging any Series 900 hours, and includes a mandatory Project Novation Clause stipulating that if the university halts or modifies the building scope (as occurred when Vanderbilt transitioned from the TEAM building to the VU ESB project), the existing project code is immediately locked and a new project code and contract addendum are executed before further work proceeds.

Second, the contract bifurcates routine building MEPF services (Schedule A) from the three experimental engineering subcomponents (Schedule B: BC-901, BC-902, and BC-903). Under Schedule B, payment of the fixed fee allocated to each experimental subcomponent is expressly contingent upon the constructed subsystem passing rigorous post-installation Field Commissioning and Performance Verification Tests—such as third-party laser vibrometry and aerosol photometer certification for BC-901. If a subsystem fails to achieve the guaranteed technical parameters, Aegis is contractually obligated to re-engineer, modify, and re-test the subsystem entirely at its own expense, and the prime architect and university retain an unconditional contractual right to withhold payment and demand a full refund of all prior milestone payments for that subsystem without limitation. Third, to satisfy Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2), the Intellectual Property clause explicitly separates the client's copyright in the stamped construction blueprints for the UTNSC facility from Aegis's ownership of the underlying engineering methodologies, parametric CFD models, custom micro-nozzle geometries, and thermodynamic discoveries, granting Aegis perpetual, royalty-free substantial rights to reuse and commercialize those research results across future client engagements without restriction.
Step 4: Granular Experimentation Time-Tracking and Substantiation Nexus

To eliminate the generic time-tracking descriptions ("design," "project coordination," "ABP") and witness impeachment that proved fatal in Phoenix Design Group, Aegis reconfigures its enterprise timekeeping system (Deltek Vantagepoint) with mandatory subcomponent validation controls. Generic discipline and phase codes are disabled for all Series 900 work. Engineers and CAD specialists must record time in real time to granular subcomponent-activity codes—such as BC-901-HYP (Hypothesis Formulation and Baseline Uncertainty Analysis), BC-901-CFD (CFD Modeling and Iterative Simulation Testing), BC-901-CAD (Experimental Prototype/BIM Modeling directly supporting CFD iterations), and BC-901-ADMIN (Non-Qualified Vendor/Architect Coordination)—accompanied by a mandatory narrative field citing the specific simulation run ID.

Crucially, when CAD designers (analogous to Barry Septer on the VU ESB steam line) or direct engineering supervisors (qualifying under Little Sandy Coal) log hours to BC-901-CAD or BC-903-CAD, the ERP system cross-validates the time entry against the Revit file version log, ensuring complete consistency between contemporaneous time logs, drawing metadata, and trial witness testimony. At year-end, this subcomponent time accounting provides an exact mathematical proof of the 80% "substantially all" test under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6): if 1,420 hours out of 1,500 total hours logged to BC-901 were recorded to HYP, CFD, and direct experimental CAD modeling, then of the activities on BC-901 constitute elements of a process of experimentation, insulating the claim from challenge.
Case Study 2: Industrial Process and Environmental Control Systems Engineering Firm
Scenario and Alignment with Phoenix Design Group Pitfalls

Vanguard Thermal & Process Systems, Inc. ("Vanguard"), a domestic engineering and turnkey process integration firm, executes 180 projects annually designing custom thermal oxidation, solvent recovery, and industrial ventilation retrofits for chemical and pharmaceutical manufacturing plants. In its flagship engagement—the High-Altitude Lithium-Ion Cathode Solvent Recovery and Thermal Oxidizer Retrofit ("Project Apex") at a facility located at an elevation of 7,200 feet—Vanguard is contracted to integrate a new regenerative thermal oxidizer (RTO) and closed-loop N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) condensation system into the plant's legacy 1980s exhaust header and chilled-water infrastructure while achieving volatile organic compound (VOC) destruction without exceeding structural roof load limits or triggering lower flammability limit (LFL) spikes.

Under PDG's flawed methodology (mirrored in the Gerald Champion project and Betz v. Commissioner), Vanguard would claim that reviewing legacy plant drawings, correcting fan airflow curves for 7,200-foot elevation air density, choosing between a local standalone chiller and the plant's central chilled-water system, sizing ductwork to comply with EPA and fire codes, and statistically extrapolating a 20-project consultant interview sample across all 180 projects qualifies for the IRC § 41 credit. Under Phoenix Design Group, such a claim would be highly vulnerable to full disallowance—the Court treated performing basic calculations on available data and selecting among options based on professional expertise as falling short of investigative activities and a process of experimentation, gave no weight to undeveloped building-code arguments, and (in PDG's case) imposed accuracy-related penalties by operation of the parties' stipulation.
Step 1: Segregating Routine Brownfield Tie-In Calculations from Genuine Process Uncertainties

To remedy these vulnerabilities, Vanguard establishes a formal Technical Eligibility Gatekeeping Protocol administered jointly by its Vice President of Engineering and tax counsel to filter out routine brownfield engineering before any project or subcomponent is chartered for R&D credit tracking. Vanguard's governance policy explicitly classifies four categories of work on Project Apex as Non-Qualified Routine Engineering: correcting volumetric airflow (CFM to ACFM) for 7,200-foot barometric pressure using standard psychrometric charts; calculating existing pipe and duct friction losses to choose between tying into the central chilled-water plant versus specifying an off-the-shelf local refrigeration unit; verifying structural roof loads and NFPA fire code clearances; and coordinating equipment room aesthetics or spatial footprints with plant architects.

Having excluded all routine tie-in work, Vanguard isolates the single physical subcomponent where existing engineering methods and vendor specifications genuinely fail: the Dual-Phase Cryo-Condensation and Catalytic Venturi Mixing Chamber ("Business Component V-400"). Because low atmospheric partial pressure at 7,200 feet causes NMP solvent vapor to nucleate into sub-micron aerosols (mist) that bypass conventional packed-bed condensers and cause flashback detonation in standard RTO ceramic beds, neither available thermodynamic literature nor commercial vendor data establish an appropriate design or method to capture of the sub-micron aerosol at high altitude while keeping system pressure drop below .
Step 2: Implementing a Scientific-Method Experimental Protocol

To prove that its engineers engaged in a scientific process of experimentation rather than exercising "general professional expertise" or following a linear design checklist, Vanguard executes and documents a multi-iteration experimental protocol for Business Component V-400. At the outset, Vanguard engineers document three competing technical hypotheses to coalesce and strip sub-micron NMP aerosols under low barometric pressure: Alternative 1, utilizing supersonic converging-diverging Venturi nozzle injection with sub-cooled recirculated solvent to induce heterogeneous droplet growth; Alternative 2, integrating a high-voltage corona-discharge electrostatic precipitator directly upstream of a sintered-metal micro-fin heat exchanger; and Alternative 3, employing multi-stage acoustic standing-wave agglomeration coupled with a hydrophobic polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) chevron mist eliminator.

Rather than performing basic spreadsheet sizing on known equations, Vanguard engineers build dynamic non-equilibrium multiphase process simulations in Aspen Plus and ChemCAD, and subsequently fabricate a scaled Slip-Stream Pilot Test Module installed on an active exhaust line at the client's 7,200-foot facility. Over 18 documented pilot test runs, engineers record empirical measurements of droplet size distribution via laser diffraction, LFL sensor fluctuations, static pressure drop, and VOC breakthrough using flame ionization detectors (FID). When Alternative 1 exhibits excessive pressure drop () and Alternative 2 triggers electrical arcing hazards during LFL spikes, the Contemporaneous Experimental Test Logs capture the exact empirical failure data and document the systematic tuning of Alternative 3's acoustic transducer frequency (from to ) and baffle geometry until the recovery threshold is achieved.
Step 3: Contractual Risk Allocation and Elimination of Unsubstantiated Extrapolation

To insulate the claim against both funded research challenges under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662, Vanguard reforms both its commercial contracting and its tax study methodology. Contractually, Vanguard structures the Business Component V-400 engagement as a lump-sum Turnkey Process Performance Agreement under which final customer acceptance and payment of the V-400 engineering fee are strictly conditioned upon passing a 72-hour continuous EPA Method 25A emissions and solvent-recovery acceptance test. If Business Component V-400 fails to achieve VOC destruction at pressure drop, Vanguard is legally obligated to re-engineer or remove the chamber at its sole cost and refund all prior milestone payments to the client without cap. Furthermore, the contract vests exclusive patent, trade secret, and commercial reuse rights to the acoustic-agglomeration Venturi chamber design in Vanguard.

Methodologically, Vanguard terminates its prior consultant's practice of sampling 20 projects retrospectively and extrapolating QREs across 180 projects without underlying activity records—an approach that, in PDG's case, left the taxpayer unable to substantiate qualified research at trial and, under the parties' stipulation, exposed it to accuracy-related penalties. In its place, Vanguard institutes a strict Bottom-Up Subcomponent Substantiation Policy, claiming QREs only on discrete subcomponents where a formal Subcomponent R&D Charter (Form R&D-101) was executed contemporaneously at project inception, backed by dedicated WBS subcomponent time-tracking codes, baseline uncertainty proofs, and archived simulation or pilot-test logs.
Step 4: Audit-Ready Substantiation File Assembly and Reasonable Cause Defense

Prior to filing its federal corporate income tax return and IRS Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities), Vanguard compiles a self-contained Contemporaneous R&D Tax Credit Audit Binder for Business Component V-400, satisfying IRC § 6001 and establishing an unassailable reasonable-cause and good-faith defense against IRC § 6662 penalties under IRC § 6664(c).

body.text: 5. Strategic Synthesis for United States Tax Practitioners

The United States Tax Court's decision in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113, solidifies a decisive judicial shift in federal R&D tax credit jurisprudence. Read alongside Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), and Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84, Judge Greaves' opinion confirms that the Tax Court will rigorously reject retrospective research credit studies that bundle entire custom-engineered buildings or industrial facilities into monolithic business components, equate standard multi-stage professional design workflows with the scientific method, or rely on generic time-tracking descriptions and uncorroborated trial testimony.

For United States engineering, architectural, software, and manufacturing taxpayers, sustaining an IRC § 41 research credit claim requires integrating legal and technical substantiation directly into daily project operations. Taxpayers must define business components at the discrete subcomponent level from project inception rather than claiming whole-building or whole-project hours and expecting the Tax Court to perform an unassisted shrinking-back rescue at trial. At the outset of each chartered subcomponent, engineering teams must contemporaneously document the specific technical information that is unavailable and demonstrate why standard industry equations, historical data, and building codes cannot establish an appropriate design. Throughout execution, taxpayers must preserve quantitative simulation, modeling, or prototype test records proving the systematic evaluation of competing technical alternatives, link every CAD drawing revision to an underlying experimental test, enforce subcomponent-specific time tracking strictly within active contract periods, and structure commercial agreements so that compensation depends on technical performance while preserving substantial rights in the resulting innovations.

metaDescription: Phoenix Design Group v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113: none of three sample projects was qualified research; routine design calculations fell short.
